 Springdale voter casts ballot in support of farmers
 By Antoinette Grajeda - Tuesday November 3, 2026 6:36 pm 
 https://arkansasadvocate.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20261103_MarisolCastorena_ArkansasAdvocate.mp3 
 Listen to Springdale resident Marisol Castorena discuss her reason for voting with the Arkansas Advocate’s Antoinette Grajeda. 
 At the Elmdale Baptist Church polling location in Springdale, Marisol Castorena said she was glad to hear that more young people were voting.  
 The 31-year-old microbiologist said it’s important for younger generations to understand that “your vote matters,” and it starts with local races. 
 Castorena said she cast her vote for Democrat Hallie Shoffner, who’s trying to unseat Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton. Castorena said she’s “really concerned for farmers” and hopes Shoffner will be able to help.  
 The Springdale resident said she’s also concerned about the effect of rising prices on her peers who have to work second jobs.  
 “It’s hard because you want to be able to enjoy your life, but sometimes you can’t because you have to pay your bills,” she said.

 Library funding vote overshadows other issues in one Arkansas community
 By Tess Vrbin - 6:04 pm 
 Jeremy Raines of northeastern Saline County voted for Republican candidates at the East End Baptist Church polling place on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Voters in typically Republican Saline County will decide Tuesday whether to preserve or cut the property taxes that support the local library system. 
 If Issue 5 passes, the operating budget for the library’s three branches would lose about $1.4 million. County residents have been organizing against it , but two voters in East End said Tuesday afternoon that they were under the impression a vote for Issue 5 was a vote for funding the library. 
 “If we don’t have some kind of relief for the libraries, they’re going to go away,” said Kim Lumsden, who voted for Democrats in as many contested races as possible. 
 On his way into the East End Baptist Church polling place, Jimmie Reynolds said he initially intended to vote for Issue 5 but would read it closely before voting because he believed the library should remain fully funded. 
 Reynolds said he would vote Republican down the ballot this year. He disliked the “socialist kind of talk going on with a lot of Democrats” in other states, though he also said Arkansas Democrats don’t appear to have socialist leanings. 
 Democrats running for Arkansas’ state and federal offices have attempted to tie their incumbent GOP opponents to President Donald Trump and capitalize on his growing unpopularity. 
 Reynolds said he prioritizes policy stances over a candidate’s character. While he “wouldn’t want to be in the same room with [Trump] for very long,” Reynolds said he believes Trump has “gotten a lot done” and has “more to do.” 
 Julia Johnston said she also supports Arkansas’ incumbent Republicans for reelection, including Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders. She said she didn’t know much about the Democrats running for federal office this year: Hallie Shoffner, who’s challenging U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton, and Chris Jones, who’s challenging U.S. Rep. French Hill. 
 The Republican members of Congress and their allies have run a series of attack ads against their opponents, portraying Jones as financially corrupt and Shoffner as against conservatives’ stance on immigration control. 
 Johnston said the ads made her uncomfortable enough with Jones and Shoffner that she voted for Hill and Cotton. 
 “Since I don’t know anybody that knows her personally, I don’t know how much of it’s true and how much of it’s not,” Johnston said about the ads against Shoffner. “But I didn’t feel comfortable voting outside of what I already knew.” 
 Regarding Issue 5, Johnston said she voted against it because “we need the libraries.” Jeremy Raines, a Republican voter, said he supported Issue 5 because he supports lower taxes. 
 Raines said one of his reasons for supporting Cotton over Shoffner was the fact that Shoffner has not spoken against transgender people using bathrooms and competing in sports corresponding to their stated gender identity. 
 “I just had to support the Republican incumbents over the Democratic candidates,” he said.

 Republican splits his vote between Shoffner, Hill
 By Ainsley Platt - 5:21 pm 
 Jared Saeler, a senior at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock studying nursing, holds a sign for Democratic Senate hopeful Hallie Shoffner near a Little Rock polling place on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Jared Saeler, a senior studying nursing at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock, said he is a registered Republican who split his ticket to vote for Democratic Senate hopeful Hallie Shoffner and Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill. Republicans have grown too extreme, Saeler said, and he expressed particular discontent with how Immigration and Customs Enforcement has treated immigrants since President Donald Trump returned to office last year. He said he also disliked how campaign ads released by Cotton took things Shoffner said “way out of context.” Shoffner has sought to win support from disillusioned Republicans as well as Democrats in her efforts to unseat Cotton. In a recent ad , Shoffner says that “you don’t have to change your party to want to change your senator.”  “The way that Republicans are treating people and literally separating families, throwing out American citizens, I think it’s absolutely ridiculous,” Saeler said while holding a sign for Shoffner outside a downtown Little Rock polling site as a volunteer for her campaign. He also didn’t like how Cotton opposed a bill that would make daylight saving time permanent either, saying it was evidence he wasn’t doing what Arkansans wanted him to do. Despite voting for Shoffner, Saeler still considers himself a Republican, but said he plans to vote for the person instead of the party going forward. That was why he voted for Hill. “I had a hard time voting for Chris (Jones) because he is so openly pro-choice, which is a problem for me,” Saeler said. His assessment of President Donald Trump’s second-term performance was blunt: “Terrible.” “Just look at our economy. Look at gas. Look at Iran. Like none of it is adding up,” Saeler, a 2024 Trump voter. “He’s not fulfilling any promises.”
 He said he wouldn’t vote for the president again if he could redo 2024. Instead, he said he likely wouldn’t have voted at all.

 Washington County Democrats hopeful about party’s chances
 By Antoinette Grajeda - 4:30 pm 
 https://arkansasadvocate.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20261103_Election_CourtneyKing_ArkansasAdvocate.mp3 
 Listen to Democratic candidates Rachel Eubanks, Courtney King and Stephanie Shufelt talk to the Arkansas Advocate’s Antoinette Grajeda as they pause their election work for a lunch break on a Fayetteville restaurant’s rooftop on Nov. 3, 2026.
 Democrats Courtney King, Stephanie Shufelt and Rachel Eubanks hosted an “election watch party lunch date” on a Fayetteville restaurant’s rooftop Tuesday afternoon. The luncheon provided an opportunity to refuel after the trio spent the morning checking in on polling sites around the county.  
 King is seeking to unseat Republican Rep. Chad Puryear in the Arkansas House District 25 race. Shufelt and Eubanks are also running against Republican incumbents Justice of the Peace Kyle Lyons and County Collector Angela Wood, respectively. 
 The three candidates said they’re feeling hopeful about Democrats’ chances of gaining seats across the state.
 While collecting signatures to be on the ballot, King said Democratic, Republican and Independent voters signed her petition. 
 “So that tells me right off from the very beginning that people are wanting something new and different,” King said. “So that to me is very encouraging.” 
 Likewise, Eubanks comes from a family of farmers in eastern Arkansas and said she’s been surprised to see several people in that region displaying signs in support of Hallie Shoffner, the Democrat running against Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton. Libertarian Jeff Wadlin is also running for the seat.  
 “I think that people are finally, they’re finally breaking up with party orthodoxy and they’re putting people first,” Eubanks said. “And I think that maybe the spell is kind of broken that was over them a little bit.” 
 Last updated: 4:32 pm
 At Arkansas museum serving as voting site, poll workers say getting involved a civic duty
 By Ainsley Platt - 3:58 pm 
 Poll workers Rose Barnes (left), Marck Beggs (center) and Evelyn Behrle (right) at the Historic Arkansas Museum polling site in downtown Little Rock on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate) 
 In downtown Little Rock, the stream of voters at the precinct based in the Historic Arkansas Museum had slowed as rain pounded down outside. The precinct was staffed with veteran and new poll workers who told the Advocate during a lull in the stream of voters that they felt getting involved with election work was a civic duty.
 Rose Barnes, a first-time poll worker and retired elementary school teacher, said she previously volunteered for candidates. But after doing that for a while, Barnes said she wanted to know “how the whole process goes.”
 Poll workers are essential to the smooth operation of Arkansas’ 2,000-plus voting precincts. They are required to undergo training and can’t be paid employees of campaigns or political parties.
 Sitting next to Barnes was Marck Beggs, another retired teacher who has been volunteering as an election worker since 2018. He felt it was his civic duty.
 “I started hearing that people were getting intimidated, and I’m just not very intimidated,” Beggs said.
 Evelyn Behrle, a consistent early voter, has been working at the polls the longest of the three — 10 years — starting after she retired. Like Beggs, she said it was her civic duty to do so.
 “Then someone made a comment to me about, ‘Well, if you’re going to early vote, you’re going to be retired, go help,’” Behrle said.
 A vote here signs points voters to the Historic Arkansas Musuem in downtown Little Rock, Arkansas on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Last updated: 4:05 pm
 North Pulaski County voters offer varying views on state and federal races
 By Tess Vrbin - 3:30 pm 
 Mike Huston voted on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at North Pulaski United Methodist Church in Sherwood, Arkansas. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Mike Huston of Sherwood said he voted for Democrats down the ballot in a typically Republican part of Pulaski County. 
 After voting Tuesday at North Pulaski United Methodist Church, Huston said he didn’t want to support candidates who “seem to be just in it for their own wealth.” 
 He said he particularly wanted to vote against U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton and Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders. Both are closely aligned with President Donald Trump, whose low approval has put many Republicans on the defense in the midterms.  
 Huston said he also voted against U.S. Rep. French Hill, who has represented central Arkansas for 12 years. Hill’s Democratic challenger, Chris Jones, lost to Sanders in the 2022 governor’s race, and Huston said he has now voted for Jones twice. 
 Michael Merritt, also of Sherwood, had a different perspective on Hill, Cotton and their challengers. Merritt said he is an independent but voted for Republicans this year. He said he disliked that Jones has run both for governor and for Congress in the past four years because “all that tells me is you’re looking for power.” 
 Cotton’s Democratic opponent, Hallie Shoffner, is a sixth-generation Arkansan who closed her family’s farm last year under financial strain she attributes to the Trump administration. Her Senate bid is her first time running for office, and Merritt said he was suspicious of this. 
 “Shoffner parachuted in from nowhere, and all of a sudden she’s a farm girl from Arkansas, born and raised,” Merritt said. “All that could be true… I’ve never heard of her, so I went with Cotton, although I’m not a big Cotton fan.” 
 North Pulaski County voters also have a choice between Republican state Rep. Brandon Achor and Democrat Allison Grigsby Sweatman for the region’s open state Senate seat. Republican Sen. Jane English has reached her term limit, and Sweatman unsuccessfully challenged her in 2022. 
 Merritt said Achor already holding elected office influenced his vote for him. 
 Dan Darnell, who voted at Maumelle’s First United Methodist Church, said he preferred Sweatman over Achor partly because Sweatman opposes Arkansas’ school voucher program. 
 “It didn’t do, in my opinion, what it was sold as,” Darnell said. 
 Arkansas Republicans who support the program, including Sanders and Achor, have said allowing families to choose where their children attend school will make the education system more equitable. However, most children receiving school vouchers already attended private schools. 
 Last updated: 4:02 pm
 A look at early voting turnout by county
 By Ainsley Platt - 3:00 pm 
 Counties across Arkansas saw spikes in early voting on Friday and Monday to bring the number of early votes cast in the state to 605,000. That doesn’t include the 10,559 absentee voting ballots that have been turned in so far.
 In all, nearly 150,000 ballots were cast across the last three days of early voting, of which two of those days had shorter hours. Northwest Arkansas’ Benton County saw more than 8,000 people cast ballots both days, with the total number of ballots cast across the final three days of early voting eclipsing 19,000.
 Last updated: 4:01 pm
 Rainy weather not deterring voters or campaigners
 By Advocate Staff - 2:30 pm 
 A rainy Election Day forecast didn’t deter Arkansas voters casting their ballots, nor did it keep campaign workers making last-minute appeals away.
 Here’s a look at the scene around Little Rock today.
 Voters wait to cast ballots at Second Presbyterian Church in West Little Rock on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate) A campaign volunteer, Janet Udouj braves rain while smiling at passing potential voters outside second Presbyterian Church in west Little Rock on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate) A campaign volunteer holds signs up at the intersection of Broadway Street and West Markham Street in downtown Little Rock on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Last updated: 2:30 pm
 Smooth sailing at busy Springdale polling site
 By Antoinette Grajeda - 2:00 pm 
 A Washington County voter waits to check in at the Springdale Civic Center on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate) 
 More than 300 Arkansans voted Tuesday morning at the Springdale Civic Center, one of Washington County’s 40 vote centers .  
 There was a long line during the first two hours of voting, and activity began picking back up around 10:45 a.m., according to poll worker Rachael Alagna. The 27-year-old Springdale resident said she became a poll worker two years ago to help and to inspire others her age to participate in the election process.  
 Fayetteville resident Leigh Turner served as a poll watcher at the Springdale Civic Center polling site on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Fayetteville resident Leigh Turner served as a poll watcher for the state Democratic Party and agreed things were running smoothly Tuesday morning.  
 Turner said the state’s Democratic Party asked her to observe the polling site because there are concerns about election interference with the U.S. Department of Justice sending election monitors to Washington and Pulaski counties.  
 Both counties’ election commissions voted not to allow the federal monitors inside local polling sites. Turner said she had not seen any of the DOJ workers Tuesday morning.  
 https://arkansasadvocate.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20261103_Election_LeighTurner_ArkansasAdvocate.mp3 
 Listen to poll monitor Leigh Turner discuss her concern about DOJ election monitors with the Arkansas Advocate’s Antoinette Grajeda. 
 Turner, who cast her ballot on the first day of early voting, said there were lots of issues to consider as a voter. 
 “Everything’s top of mind,” she said. “I think we need to vote to save democracy.” 
 Last updated: 2:06 pm
 The other big results coming tonight…
 By Andrew DeMillo - 1:34 pm 
 It’s a rough night to be a politico and a college football fan.
 Tuesday isn’t just Election Day. It’s also the night when the first College Football Playoff rankings of the season come out. As The Associated Press reports, the CFP puts out six sets of rankings every season on a strict schedule.
 That schedule puts it on the same night as when many voters are going to be up late focused on election results. The final set of playoff rankings come out on the first Sunday in December. You can find the rest of the rankings release schedule here .
 Last updated: 1:34 pm
 Sherwood voter says he’s driven by Cotton’s stances on social issues 
 By Tess Vrbin - 1:30 pm 
 Ronnie Ruple of Sherwood, pictured behind his truck in the parking lot at Brockington Road Church of the Nazarene, said he votes his conscience as a born-again Christian and considers “life issues” more important than the costs of gasoline and groceries. Ruple voted for Republican candidates in the midterm election Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Ronnie Ruple of Sherwood said voting is “a matter of conscience” instead of “dollars and cents and nuts and bolts” outside the polling place at Brockington Road Church of the Nazarene. 
 As a born-again Christian and longtime Republican, Ruple said his priorities at the ballot box are “life issues,” such as his opposition to abortion, same-sex marriage and transgender people’s access to bathrooms and locker rooms that correspond with their gender identity. 
 He said Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton, who’s running for a third term, earned his vote by being clear about his opposition to the same things while his Democratic opponent, Hallie Shoffner, “has not been very forthcoming” about where she stands on transgender rights. 
 One of Shoffner’s consistent messages has been her opposition to elected officials using their positions to enrich themselves. 
 Ruple said he shares that opposition, “but that is something that’s not on the ballot.” 
 “We have to accept the fact that God knows all things, that he’s watching over all things, and that we do our part by doing the next right thing,” Ruple said. “And voting your conscience, I think, is more important than the price of gas or how much it costs me for a sack of groceries.” 
 Last updated: 1:37 pm
 Affordability big concern in east Springdale House district
 By Antoinette Grajeda - 1:05 pm 
 Matt Goff, Republican candidate for Arkansas House District 9, holds campaign signs with his family outside the Springdale Civic Center on Nov. 3, 2026. Pictured are Goff’s daughter, Hannah White, and his grandkids, Samuel, Selah and Stephen White, and Annabelle and Lydia Wascura. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Republican Matt Goff and his family held campaign signs outside the Springdale Civic Center as the wind picked up Tuesday morning.  
 Goff is running against Democratic Rep. Diana Gonzales Worthen in the Arkansas House District 9 race. In 2022, Gonzales Worthen flipped the east Springdale seat, which is the state’s only Latino-majority district.  
 https://arkansasadvocate.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20261103_Election_MattGoff_ArkansasAdvocate.mp3 
 Listen to Republican House District 9 candidate Matt Goff talk about his campaign with the Arkansas Advocate’s Antoinette Grajeda. 
 Goff, a retired Army veteran with 7 kids and 22 grandkids, said he’s been knocking doors for the last eight weeks. He’s met several voters who have concerns about affordability.  
 “The pressure of things going up, that’s probably the number one thing people talk about — from housing to food,” he said. 
 Voters have also voiced concerns about school choice and “the government not being responsive to the people,” Goff said.
 Last updated: 1:32 pm
 What’s happening in neighboring states
 By Andrew DeMillo - 12:30 pm 
 Arkansas has had heated races for statewide and congressional offices this year, but the spending and attention has been much greater in neighboring states.
 Texas’ election has been dominated by the expensive race for U.S. Senate between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton. Check out the Texas Tribune’s coverage of the Texas election matchups.
 The midterm environment has even created a potentially competitive race for U.S. Senate in solidly Republican Mississippi. Mississippi Today has a rundown of the election there. And here’s a look at how our colleagues at the Tennessee Lookout are covering their election.
 Last updated: 12:33 pm
 A split-ticket voter in Little Rock says officials aren’t doing their jobs
 By Ainsley Platt - 12:09 pm 
 Hyman Williams of Little Rock is a Vietnam War veteran and a split-ticket voter. After voting at the Dunbar Community Center Tuesday, he said elected officials weren’t doing their jobs, pointing to potholes and long wait time to fix a downed traffic light.
 “I voted for French Hill because he’s more affiliated with the veterans and knows what they need,” Williams, a longtime Pulaski County voter, said. “And Frank Scott, I voted for him because he seemed like he doing a good job. But still, all those people in the office need to be evaluated.”

 A heated, personal race for state House plays out in Maumelle
 By Tess Vrbin - 11:51 am 
 BJ Saunders waves a sign supporting Republican state House candidate Stephen Bright outside the First United Methodist Church polling place in Maumelle on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate) 
 BJ Saunders has been involved in Maumelle politics for years since her husband is a former city councilman, she said. 
 But what led her to wave signs on the sidewalks of Edgewood Drive outside the First United Methodist Church polling place Tuesday were the abuse and voter fraud allegations against Stephen Bright, the Republican running for Maumelle’s open state House seat. 
 Bright represented Maumelle in the House from 2003 to 2011. Saunders has lived in the city since 2000, and her familiarity with him leads her to believe “he’s the best man for the job,” she said. 
 Cassandra Mayes, Bright’s Democratic opponent, accused Bright of voting illegally in Maumelle despite not living there. Bright refuted the accusation , saying that not changing his registration was “a simple oversight during a move” to Little Rock and that his registration became accurate again when he moved back to Maumelle. 
 Democrats have criticized Bright following reports of court documents that claimed abusive behavior toward his ex-wife, current wife and children. 
 Saunders said the accusations were “dirty pool” and “not playing fair.” She said she believes Bright has earned Maumelle residents’ trust. 
 Bright and Mayes are running to succeed Republican Rep. Brandon Achor, who’s running for state Senate against Democrat Allison Grigsby Sweatman. Mayes unsuccessfully challenged Achor in 2024. 
 Achor withdrew his endorsement of Bright following the allegations in the court documents. 
 Achor has recently been airing ads featuring former Gov. Asa Hutchinson , who has endorsed his Senate bid.  
 Edgewood Drive has been lined for weeks with signs for local, state and federal candidates of both major parties, as well as Libertarian and nonpartisan candidates. Saunders said she’s seen more enthusiasm for Tuesday’s election than previous ones. 
 “I think people are wanting America to go the right way,” she said. 
 Signs supporting a variety of candidates line the sidewalk outside the First United Methodist Church polling place in Maumelle, Arkansas on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Last updated: 1:26 pm
 Arkansas’ election could break racial barriers at state and local level
 By Andrew DeMillo - 11:30 am 
 Arkansas is the only former Confederate state that hasn’t elected a Black person to Congress. That distinction could change on Tuesday. 
 If he wins in central Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District and unseats Republican Rep. French Hill , Chris Jones would make history as the state’s first African-American congressman. The race is the most competitive among the state’s four congressional districts and has been targeted by national Democrats. 
 Democratic congressional nominee Chris Jones voting with his daughters Janelle (13, left) and Jasmine (10, right) at the Pulaski County early voting site in downtown Little Rock on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Jones is running against Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill in the 2nd Congressional District (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate) 
 The race is among several races where Black candidates could make history in Arkansas. 
 Democratic state Sen. Fred Love is hoping to be the state’s first Black governor as he challenges Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders . 
 In Pulaski County, Democrat Wendell Griffen could become the first Black person elected to lead Arkansas’ most populous county. 
 Meanwhile, Little Rock Mayor Frank Scott is seeking a third term leading Arkansas’ capital. Scott, who is being challenged by City Director B.J. Wyrick, became the first popularly elected Black mayor of the city in 2018. 
 Last updated: 11:31 am
 Politics may divide us. ‘I Voted’ stickers don’t.
 By Andrew DeMillo - 10:30 am 
 A stack of “I voted” stickers sits on a vote tabulator at the Pulaski County Regional Building during early voting on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026 in Little Rock, Arkansas. (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate) 
 Arkansas voters may disagree on who they’ll vote for Tuesday, but displaying the “I voted” sticker is a bipartisan affair.
 The stickers poll workers hand to voters after they cast a ballot Tuesday will be a common sight around Arkansas and the rest of the country. The sticker you get will depend on where you’re voting.
 In Washington County, voters will receive stickers hand-crafted by two local students that were selected in a contest. Pulaski County voters will receive traditional red-white-and-blue “I voted” stickers.
